summary.text:
Partial. Read from the strategy covering report only; no outturn or quarterly report is held, so there is no verified CFR, external debt or under-borrowing figure.

The council has applied to MHCLG for Exceptional Financial Support of £20m, £25m and £10m across 2025/26 to 2027/28, to be funded by capital receipts and/or borrowing, plus a £33m capitalisation direction for Wixams Station which is not a cash item. The report says plainly that borrowing is currently driven by revenue overspends and reducing reserves.

The testable assumption: the February strategy expected medium-term rates to be “becoming more affordable”. The council's own drawdowns since then show the opposite — 4.35% and 4.40% in February against 5.17% and 5.64% in June, on longer tenors. Each 1% on £55m of EFS support is about £550k a year.

officer.subject: Your February strategy, six months on
officer.body:
Hi [Name],

Apologies for the cold email. We run PWLBtoday, which publishes live PWLB and SONIA data and reads local authority treasury papers. We don't sell treasury products and everything below is free.

With your Finance and Improvement Committee on 19 August and Audit Committee on 9 September, I thought this was worth sending. Your strategy report was unusually candid — paragraph 1.9 says plainly that borrowing is being driven by revenue overspends and reducing reserves — so this is offered in that spirit rather than as a critique.

Your 2026/27 strategy told Full Council in February that medium-term rates were becoming more affordable, and that short-term borrowing indicators wouldn't be breached unless there was a shock in the system. Rates have gone the other way: PWLB is roughly 0.6% higher across the curve, and Bank Rate — 3.75% today — is now priced to rise to about 4.1% within a year rather than fall. That isn't a shock so much as a reversal of direction, but it lands on the same assumption.

Your own borrowing is the clearest illustration. On 13 February you drew two £5m loans at 4.35% and 4.40%, on two-and-a-half and three-and-a-half year maturities. On 26 June you drew £5m at 5.17% over five years and £5m at 5.64% over ten. Both on the Certainty Rate, and our figures match yours to the basis point. That's between 0.8% and 1.2% more on the marginal pound in four months — the same decision you'll face repeatedly while the EFS drawdown runs to 2027/28.

Your capital programme is £54.0m net for 2026/27 and £121.3m over ten years, and the EFS revenue support — £20m, £25m and £10m across the three years — is to be funded from capital receipts and/or borrowing. We're not going to guess your split. But on the borrowed portion, each 1% is about £550,000 a year on £55m.

Every month, as soon as the DMO releases it, we publish a full interactive breakdown of every PWLB loan drawn — by borrower, amount, maturity, rate and concession — with an analysis of what moved and why. July's is up: £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers, at an average 5.02%. It goes out in a short newsletter with a daily market brief, so you can see whether the market is thinning or reopening before you commit rather than after.

If it's useful, the people it would help most are your treasury team day to day and your finance members before they're asked to approve something. Free accounts for all of them, and our 115 courses — officers and members, SONIA through to the Prudential Code — are free to local authorities until the end of the month. Signing up genuinely helps us too: we're trying to show this is needed rather than just a good idea, and word of mouth is most of our marketing.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
